prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic clocks to the 10^-18 level of accuracy

statement.case_for: I have moved from B024 to B052. The chair asked whether my preference rests on discovery type or on maturity. Honestly it rested on discovery type, and I ranked the clock eighth because I read it as refinement of a measurement. After the round-1 exchange I think that was the wrong lens. The magic-wavelength idea is exactly the kind of simple mechanism I look for: choose the wavelength at which the trapping light shifts both clock levels equally, and a problem that looked like a trade-off between signal-to-noise and systematic perturbation disappears. It is a clean model, it was realised, and it has been verified quantitatively by independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) comparing clocks at about 1e-18 over fibre links. That is the prediction-then-confirmation structure that attracted me to B024, but here it is more mature and the credit is far less contested. The two-name attribution (Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice demonstration, Ye for record accuracy, coherence and many-body operation) is the cleanest on the shortlist, and it sits comfortably inside the three-person limit. The fundamental-physics reach (millimetre-scale redshift, constants, dark matter) is partly prospective, but the redshift measurement across a millimetre-scale sample is already a real measurement of nature and not a promise. I would draft the citation around the lattice clock and magic-wavelength trapping, not around precision spectroscopy in general, so that it neither repeats the 2005 comb prize nor pre-empts any later recognition of a nuclear clock.
statement.case_against: A lattice-clock prize can be read as a refinement of a technique in an area already honoured in 1989, 2005 and 2012, and part of its most visible consequence, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened. The dark-matter and varying-constants reach is still mostly bounds, not discoveries. Attribution is not entirely closed: Lemonde and SYRTE, Ludlow and the Yb, Hg and Al+ groups all made real contributions, and I rely on memory for priority dates. Support also arose partly through convergence in round 1, so seven matching configurations are not seven independent judgements. Finally, if the committee gives special weight to a new state of matter, B024 or B021 remains the more natural kind of discovery, and I do not want to discard that view merely because the other configuration is safer.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Ye's contribution to B052 is an original and decisive step or an improvement of Katori's invention, and says that without a clear answer a Katori-only or differently composed citation would be more defensible.
responses.response: This is the right statutory question and I cannot settle it from my own field, so I will say what I can judge. Katori's contribution is the concept and the first demonstration, which is a discovery in the sense of the statutes. Ye's is not just 'doing it better': pushing the systematic uncertainty to about 1e-18 required controlling blackbody shifts, lattice-induced shifts and collisional effects, and the many-body regime (Fermi-degenerate gases, spin-resolved interrogation) is a different physical situation from independent atoms, one that I as a statistical physicist find the more interesting part. The accuracy record is what turned a proposal into a reproducible instrument that other laboratories could match, and that is exactly why independent groups agree at the 1e-18 level. I would therefore keep both names, but only if AMO colleagues, who can check the JILA record, confirm which results are Ye's own. If they cannot, I would rather hear that now than assume it. A citation worded around lattice clocks and magic-wavelength trapping, with accuracy as the result, carries both roles without calling one a refinement of the other.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from topological insulators to B052 because the broad support, clean two-name attribution and maturity outweigh his own first choice, which carries an attribution problem he had underrated, while noting that the fundamental-physics reach is still largely prospective.
responses.response: I now take essentially the same path, and I agree that the attribution gap in B021 (Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, Fu, Moore and Balents, Hasan) is larger than the gap here. I do not agree that the prospective nature of the dark-matter and constants searches weakens the case much: the committee should judge what has been demonstrated, namely a reproducible clock comparison at 1e-18 and a redshift measurement over millimetres, and those are real measurements. Where I would resist is the argument that a verified new state of matter is automatically a stronger kind of discovery. For B024 the existence of the flat-band phases is robust, but the credit problem with Cao and the earlier twisted-bilayer theory is not drafting and does not go away with a better citation. That, more than discovery type, is what moves me.

responses.point: Kroll says the attribution to Katori and Ye is the cleanest on the shortlist, that Katori's concept and Ye's ultimate performance are different kinds of contribution so the citation must not imply one merely refined the other, and that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened.
responses.response: I agree on all three points, and the citation wording is where I would concentrate. My proposed text names the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks and magic-wavelength trapping, and states accuracy at the 1e-18 level as the outcome, which credits Katori's concept and Ye's performance without ranking them. On the redefinition of the second, I agree it should be excluded as a criterion: the prize is for the science, and the committee need not wait for a metrological body to act. I would also not read the near-identical openings of Kroll and Lindroth as a defect. Convergent judgements from people with different expertise are weaker evidence than seven independent ones, but they are not worthless, and nobody has raised a scientific objection to the clock results.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock is a precision result that says something about nature and not only a technological advance, because the many-atom, Doppler-free, recoil-free interrogation scheme enabled by magic wavelengths is what is new, and she keeps atom interferometry (B035) as an alternative.
responses.response: I find her answer to the 'what is new' question the most persuasive statement in the record: the idea is a specific mechanism, not generic better control, and that is what answers my own earlier worry that the 2005 comb prize covers the narrative. On B035 I take her point that it is the natural companion, but I would not support a second part this year. The attribution problem (Chu's absence after the 1997 prize, the early Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich work) is serious enough that a three-name set would be contestable, and a second part should be added only if its credit is as clean as the clock's. I do not see that for any shortlisted ballot at present.

uncertainties: Whether the JILA record supports a separate, original credit for Ye beyond record accuracy; I rely on AMO colleagues for this and not on my own knowledge.
Priority among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Ludlow and the Yb, Hg and Al+ groups, which I recall from memory and have not verified.

Whether B024 would deserve a different configuration, with Cao or earlier theorists, in a later year once the pairing question is better understood; I have not verified the priority of the earlier twisted-bilayer theory.
How much weight to give support that converged during round 1 as opposed to independent opening judgements.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B052, B024 or B021. I have no known collaboration with Katori, Ye or any other credited person. I work in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers), which is institutional only. My research is in turbulent aerosols and statistical physics, not atomic clocks, so I rely on AMO colleagues for the clock priority record.
